turns.content: I've been staring at the group chat for an hour. Karen's schedule has me down for kid duty every afternoon again, just like last summer. Alex says we should go but set boundaries on the call tonight. I don't think I have it in me to fight that out over the phone and then spend a week enforcing it. Would I be terrible if I just pulled out of the rental and let them figure it out?

You wouldn't be terrible. You'd be someone who looked at a schedule that already had her name penciled in as free labor and decided she didn't want to spend a week's vacation renegotiating it in real time.

A couple of things worth pulling apart, though, because they're tangled up together right now:

**The phone call vs. the week.** Alex's plan assumes the hard part is the call. You're saying the hard part is the seven days after, where every afternoon someone drifts off and you're the one left standing there deciding whether to make it a thing. That's a legitimate read, and you know Karen's patterns better than a boundary-setting strategy does. If your gut says the boundary won't hold without constant policing, that's information, not cowardice.

**A version that isn't the fight or the full exit.** You don't actually have to hash it out live. You could put one message in the group chat, in writing, something like: "I'm not doing solo kid coverage this year. If the schedule needs to shift, happy to talk, but I'm only in if afternoons are shared or covered by someone else." Then you let the reactions be theirs to have. If they adjust, great. If they get weird about it, you've learned what you needed to before putting down money and a week of your life.

**If you do pull out.** It's allowed. Money and vacation days are finite, and "I'd spend the whole trip resenting people I love" is a real reason not to go. The cost is you might feel like the one who bailed, and Karen may read it as sulking rather than a choice. You can soften that some by being plain about the why, but you can't control how she files it. That's true whether you go or not.

The question I'd actually sit with: is the dread mostly about the kid duty, or about the fact that this is the second summer running and nobody else in that chat seems to notice? Because if it's the second one, skipping the trip fixes this week but not the pattern, and it might be worth saying the pattern part out loud to Alex tonight before anything else.

Either way: an hour staring at a group chat is your body already voting. Give that some weight.

I hear you. I do. But the dread isn't just about the call—it's about being the one who has to monitor and enforce every day. That's a job, not a vacation. Alex keeps saying "set boundaries," but in practice, that means I'm the bad guy for a week straight. Doesn't it?

Yeah, mostly it does. And the part Alex is skipping is *who* plays the bad guy.

"Set boundaries" sounds like a one-time act. What you're describing is the maintenance contract: noticing at 2pm that nobody's come to take over, deciding whether today's the day you say something, saying it, absorbing the eye-roll or the "oh I thought you had them," and then doing it again tomorrow. That's emotional labor stacked on top of the childcare labor you were trying to get out of. You're right to call it a job.

But I'd push on one thing before you decide it's inevitable. The reason it's *you* for a week straight is that the plan, as Alex framed it, quietly assumes you're the enforcer. That's not baked into boundaries. It's baked into how the two of you are dividing this up. Some questions worth putting to Alex tonight, before anyone's on the phone with Karen:

- If Karen wanders off at 2pm on Tuesday, who says something? If the answer is "well, you, since it's your afternoon," then Alex is asking you to hold the line alone and calling it teamwork.
- Would Alex be willing to be the one who raises it with Karen, and the one who re-raises it mid-week? Not "backs you up." Goes first.
- Is Alex okay with the trip being a little tense, or does Alex want you to set the boundary *and* keep the peace? Because those pull against each other, and if it's the second one, that's the actual trap.

If Alex hears that and says "fair, I'll be the one who deals with Karen," the week looks different. Still not effortless, but you're not the lone cop. If Alex kind of shrugs and says "just be firm," then you've learned the boundary plan was always going to run on your battery, and pulling out stops looking like bailing and starts looking like refusing a bad deal.

One more thing: you keep saying "bad guy," and I get why. But in that group, you're only the bad guy if everyone else has agreed that you being the default sitter is neutral. It isn't. Someone deciding you're free labor is the thing that needs a villain label, not you declining it. That doesn't make the week feel better in the moment, but it might make it easier to stop apologizing in your head for wanting one.

I keep coming back to the same thing: even if Alex agrees to be the one who speaks up, I'm still the one who has to live in that house all week with Karen's mood. Boundaries sound good in theory, but they don't make the tension go away at the dinner table.

No, they don't. You're right about that, and I'm not going to pretend there's a phrasing that makes Karen pleasant about being told no.

So let me just name where you've landed, because I think you already know: there are exactly three versions of this week, and none of them is tension-free.

1. **Go, say nothing.** Kid duty every afternoon, quiet resentment, Karen's in a great mood because the arrangement works for her.
2. **Go, hold the line.** Your afternoons back, Karen's in a mood, you eat dinner next to it for seven nights.
3. **Don't go.** No kid duty, no dinner table, Karen's in a mood about it from a distance, and you're not there to feel it.

You keep testing option 2 for a version where Karen doesn't sulk, and there isn't one. Her mood isn't a design flaw in the plan. It's the price of the plan. The only real question is whether that price is worth a week at the beach with people you presumably still like at least some of the time.

And if the answer is "not this year," that's a complete answer. You don't have to prove boundaries won't work in order to be allowed to skip a vacation you're dreading. "I don't want to spend my one week off managing someone else's mood" is enough.

One thing I'd gently point out: you've now ruled out the call, the enforcement, and the atmosphere. That's not someone weighing options. That's someone who's decided and is looking for permission to have decided. You have it. The harder conversation is probably with Alex, who wants to go and may hear "I'm out" as "you're on your own with my family." That one's worth having tonight, plainly, before the group call turns it into a group problem.
I hear you. I just don't know if I can sit through that call tonight pretending I'm open to a plan I've already decided I don't want. Alex is going to be disappointed either way.

Then don't pretend. That's the one part of tonight you actually get to control.

Sitting on a group call performing openness to a plan you've already rejected is the worst of both worlds. You'd be exhausted *and* still have to tell Alex afterward. So flip the order: talk to Alex before the call, not after.

Something like: "I've decided I'm not going. I know that's not what you want to hear. I don't want to get on the call tonight acting like I'm negotiating when I'm not." Short. No case to argue, because you don't need Alex's sign-off, you need Alex to not be blindsided.

Then a couple of options for the call itself:

- **You skip it.** Alex goes on, says "she's out this year," and lets the schedule be Karen's problem. You don't owe the group a live explanation.
- **You join for two minutes.** Say it yourself, plainly, then get off. Some people feel better having said it directly rather than having it relayed. Only worth it if that's you.

On Alex being disappointed either way: yes. But there's a difference between "disappointed you're not coming" and "disappointed you let me walk into a call thinking we had a plan." The first one is just a feeling Alex gets to have. The second one is a small betrayal you can avoid entirely by talking first.

And you might name one more thing to Alex, because it matters: you're not opting out of the family, you're opting out of a week that was set up for you to be the help. Alex can go. Alex can have a good time. That's allowed too. You're not asking anyone to boycott, you're just declining your own assignment.

You're not going to feel great tonight. But you'll feel a lot less awful having said a true thing to one person than having said a fake thing to six.
I think I need to tell Alex before the call, like you said. I'll say it plainly—I'm not going. No case to argue. Then I'll skip the group call entirely. That feels cleaner.

It is cleaner. And notice how much lighter that sounded than anything you said an hour ago.

Two small things so it stays clean:

- **Resist the case anyway.** Alex might ask "but why not just try it?" and you'll feel the pull to relitigate. You don't have to. "I've thought about it a lot, and I'm sure" is a full sentence. Repeating it once is fine.
- **Say something about Alex going.** Even one line, "I want you to go and have a good week," takes the "are you asking me to pick sides" question off the table before it gets asked.

Then close the group chat and do literally anything else while the call happens. It's Karen's schedule to fix now.

You did the hard part already, which was deciding. Tonight's just saying it out loud.
